submissions.findingTextShort: PMID 25174896 is an infantile eye-tumor pathology paper and cannot support the current CoQ10 fatigue claim.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: The source currently attached to the CoQ10 fatigue claim, PMID 25174896 / DOI 10.1016/j.ajo.2014.08.036, is a retrospective clinicopathologic and immunohistochemical study of infantile intraocular medulloepithelioma. It does not study coenzyme Q10 supplementation, fatigue, exercise, mitochondrial supplementation, or a CoQ10 intervention and therefore cannot provide semantic support for any CoQ10 efficacy claim.
submissions.populationContext: Three infants with intraocular medulloepithelioma; an ophthalmic tumor-pathology population unrelated to CoQ10 supplementation.
submissions.usageContext: Source-contamination finding only; the publication contains no CoQ10 intervention.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Bibliographic identity is clear and the entity/intervention mismatch is direct. This staging record does not itself edit the canonical profile; the incorrect source must be removed through governed canonical repair. This source must never pass semantic attestation for CoQ10.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 13-RCT meta-analysis found a pooled fatigue-score reduction with CoQ10, with population and formulation heterogeneity.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2022 systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 13 randomized controlled trials totaling 1,126 participants found lower fatigue scores with CoQ10 versus placebo (Hedges' g -0.398, 95% CI -0.641 to -0.155). Included studies spanned healthy and disease populations, and subgroup results differed by CoQ10-only versus mixed-compound formulations, so the pooled signal should not be converted into a universal fatigue-treatment claim or a single standard dose.
submissions.populationContext: Thirteen randomized controlled trials with 1,126 participants across healthy and disease populations.
submissions.usageContext: Oral CoQ10 interventions with varying formulations, doses, durations, and fatigue contexts; pooled fatigue evidence rather than one standardized consumer product.
submissions.safetyContext: The review reported only one gastrointestinal adverse event among 602 CoQ10 recipients, but sparse trial adverse-event reporting cannot establish comprehensive or long-term safety.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Population and formulation heterogeneity remain material. Dose and duration meta-regression associations are study-level findings and must not be converted into an individualized dosing rule. One author disclosed founding InnovaRad Inc. The source remains draft-only until canonical registration and semantic attestation are complete.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2026 depression meta-analysis found a depressive-symptom signal but no significant fatigue benefit in the two fatigue trials.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of five randomized controlled trials totaling 474 participants with primary depression or depression accompanying medical conditions found a pooled depressive-symptom improvement, but the fatigue outcome based on two trials was not significant (SMD -0.33, 95% CI -1.38 to 0.72; p=0.54) and showed very high heterogeneity (I²=89%). The depressive-symptom result and fatigue result must remain separate outcomes.
submissions.populationContext: Five randomized trials with 474 participants with depression; three trials involved major medical comorbidity and two involved primary depressive disorders.
submissions.usageContext: Depression-focused CoQ10 trials; fatigue synthesis came from only two included trials and is not a general-population fatigue estimate.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Only two trials contributed fatigue data and heterogeneity was very high, so the null estimate is imprecise rather than proof of no effect. It should remain visible alongside the broader 2022 fatigue meta-analysis instead of being averaged away or selectively omitted. The source remains draft-only until canonical registration and semantic attestation are complete.

submissions.findingTextShort: The newest exercise synthesis found reliable blood CoQ10 increases but only small, inconsistent performance effects with low certainty.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials in healthy adults found that CoQ10 supplementation reliably increased circulating CoQ10 concentrations, while exercise-performance effects were small and inconsistent. Chronic-supplementation and aerobic-endurance signals became unstable or borderline after outlier exclusion, acute effects were trivial, no stable dose-response pattern emerged, and overall certainty was rated very low to low because of heterogeneity and moderate-to-high risk of bias.
submissions.populationContext: Randomized exercise studies in healthy adults, including trained and untrained participants across differing exercise outcomes.
submissions.usageContext: Exercise-performance and subjective-fatigue context; biochemical elevation of circulating CoQ10 is an exposure marker and not proof of improved performance.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Performance findings were sensitive to analytic choices and outlier removal, and no stable dose-response pattern was found. Do not translate blood-level increases, mitochondrial plausibility, or isolated subgroup findings into a broad ergogenic claim. The source remains draft-only until canonical registration and semantic attestation are complete.
